source.version: Journal version of record: Technovation 153 (2026) 103540; received 11 November 2025, revised 3 March 2026, accepted 16 March 2026, available online 19 March 2026 (p. 1)
source.title_on_document: The role of task breadth and cognitive flexibility in generative AI-supported creative idea generation

supplement.where: The document refers to no supplementary material or online appendix. Appendices A to E (prompt, instructions, coding scheme, expert ratings, normality tests) are inside this PDF, pp. 13-19. Data availability: 'Data will be made available on request' (p. 19).

paper_design_summary: Two online between-subjects experiments on new venture idea generation. In each, participants were randomly assigned to see a few startup ideas pre-generated by a fine-tuned GPT-3 model (10 ideas in Study 1, a broad task with management master's students; 4 ideas in Study 2, a narrow EdTech task with UK Prolific entrepreneurs) or no ideas, and then wrote their own startup ideas for about 10 minutes. The scored outputs are the number of semantic categories each person's ideas span (breadth of exploration), ideas per category (depth), pairwise embedding similarity of ideas across participants, and expert ratings of novelty and usefulness (Appendix D).

studies.label: Study 1 (broad task: startup ideas in any domain, master's students)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Exposure to 10 startup ideas drawn at random from a database of 453 ideas generated by a fine-tuned GPT-3 model, shown as optional inspiration during the task, versus no ideas
assignment.quote: Ninety-three participants were randomly assigned to one of two groups: exposed to ideas generated by a fine-tuned LLM (n = 46) or no exposure to LLM-generated ideas (n = 47).
assignment.locator: p. 6, Section 4.1; also p. 8, Section 4.5 ('The participants were randomly assigned to one group.')
assignment.prereg_locator: No preregistration mentioned; an a priori G*Power analysis is reported (p. 6, Section 4.1)

arms.name: LLM-assisted human
arms.description: Saw 10 random fine-tuned-GPT-3 startup ideas on the task page as optional inspiration; told they were AI-generated and not to submit an identical idea

arms.name: Human-only
arms.description: Same scenario and instructions with no AI ideas; told they could do internet research if they wished

participants.exclusions: Three participants excluded because they failed to complete the experiment, leaving 90 (45 per group). A sensitivity analysis drops participants who failed the manipulation check (22 percent did not confirm the ideas were AI-generated); the paper says results are unchanged but prints no numbers.
participants.who: International master's students in management who had taken at least one entrepreneurship course; mean age about 23; 65 percent female; 91 percent took the study in French, 9 percent in English. Recruited by cold electronic messaging.
participants.country: not_stated (91 percent chose French; authors at SKEMA Business School, France)
participants.quote: Three participants were excluded from the final analysis because they failed to complete the experiment, leaving 90 participants.
participants.locator: p. 6, Section 4.1; p. 8, Section 4.6 ('In total, 90 participants (45 per group) generated 208 ideas.'); p. 9, Table 4

ai_tool.name_model: 'Startup Ideas powered by OpenAI' (ideasai.net, 2022), described as a fine-tuned GPT-3 model; ideas generated before the release of ChatGPT
ai_tool.how_used: 488 startup ideas were pre-generated with a prompt that lists past ideas labelled 'Good idea:' or 'Bad idea:' from online user votes (Appendix A); incoherent ideas and ideas describing existing firms were removed, leaving 453. Each treated participant saw 10 drawn at random, with no obligation to use them. Participants did not interact with the model.

task.description: Imagine applying to an incubator: submit different startup ideas likely to be funded, each giving the business need, product or service, major source of revenue, and target customer; any domain allowed (instructions in Appendix B, p. 14).
task.duration: Minimum 8 minutes, instructed to spend about 10 minutes, no maximum (p. 8, Section 4.5)

outcomes.name: Breadth of exploration
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Number of distinct semantic categories (out of 15 inductively derived categories) that a participant's ideas span. One author and an independent external researcher each assigned every idea to a category; agreement within 1 point was 99 percent, ICC (absolute agreement) 0.97; the two raters' breadth counts were averaged (p. 7, Section 4.4.1). Kruskal-Wallis test because the outcome is not normal (Appendix E); the paper says parametric tests agree. Robust to dropping manipulation-check failures (no numbers printed).

contrasts.reported: LLM-assisted human M = 2.32 (SD 1.32, N = 45) vs Human-only M = 1.60 (SD 0.74, N = 45); Cohen's d = 0.67; Kruskal-Wallis chi2(1) = 6.43, p = 0.01; significant after Holm-Bonferroni correction for the two primary outcome tests

outcomes.name: Depth of exploration
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Number of ideas divided by breadth of exploration (ideas per semantic category), read as a consequence of cognitive persistence (p. 8, Section 4.4.2). Not hypothesized ('although we did not make a hypothesis'), but the paper counts it among the 'two primary outcome tests' for the Holm-Bonferroni correction. Kruskal-Wallis test.

contrasts.reported: LLM-assisted human M = 1.13 (SD 0.26, N = 45) vs Human-only M = 1.15 (SD 0.33, N = 45); Cohen's d = 0.07; Kruskal-Wallis chi2(1) = 0.45, p = 0.50

outcomes.name: Average pairwise semantic similarity of ideas within condition
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Only the first idea of each participant kept. Text preprocessed (tokenization, stop-word and generic-word removal such as 'startup', 'idea', 'revenue', lemmatization, punctuation removal); SpaCy sentence embeddings; mean cosine similarity over all pairs of ideas within each condition. Described as exploratory, complementary analysis, not a hypothesis test. Sign reversed: lower similarity means more diversity, so the LLM arm's lower similarity is coded treatment_higher.

contrasts.reported: Cosine similarity: Human-only M = 0.81 (SD = 0.08) vs LLM-assisted M = 0.74 (SD = 0.13); M difference = 0.07, 95% CI [0.04, 0.10], p = 0.00, Cohen's d = 0.91 (permutation test, 10,000 iterations). Table 7: N (ideas) = 45 per arm; permutation p = 0.00. Note: 'mean_difference_se' stands for a mean difference with a CI; no SE is printed.

diversity_detail.metric: Mean pairwise cosine similarity of sentence embeddings within condition (higher = more homogeneous)
diversity_detail.computed_over: All pairs of ideas within a condition, using each participant's first idea only (45 ideas per arm)
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Permutation test with 10,000 iterations on the difference in mean within-group similarity; 95% CI and Cohen's d reported
diversity_detail.notes: The paper also compares human-only ideas with the pool of LLM-generated stimuli (M difference = -0.10, 95% CI [-0.12, -0.09], p = 0.00, d = -1.74; p. 8), an AI-versus-human comparison not coded as an outcome here.

outcomes.name: Average novelty (expert ratings)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Consensual Assessment Technique: each idea rated by at least two of six expert judges (entrepreneurship, innovation, intrapreneurship) on seven-point scales; novelty = newness, uniqueness, unusualness. Agreement within 1.5 points: 68.4 percent for novelty. Idea scores averaged across judges, then across a participant's ideas. Described as descriptive and exploratory; no test reported.

contrasts.reported: LLM-assisted human 3.90 (0.79, 45) vs Human-only 3.97 (0.72, 45), M (SD, N); no test reported; direction is the point estimate only

outcomes.name: Average usefulness (expert ratings)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Same judges and procedure as novelty; usefulness = feasibility and operability items (a third item, read by judges as viability, 'was dropped after Study 1 due to low internal consistency'; the text does not say whether the Study 1 score includes it). Agreement within 1.5 points: 65.5 percent. No test reported.

contrasts.reported: LLM-assisted human 4.57 (0.54, 45) vs Human-only 4.73 (0.69, 45), M (SD, N); no test reported; direction is the point estimate only

outcomes.name: Average creativity (mean of expert novelty and usefulness)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Composite: mean of the novelty and usefulness ratings, not a separate holistic rating. Agreement within 1.5 points: 84.6 percent. No test reported.

contrasts.reported: LLM-assisted human 4.23 (0.37, 45) vs Human-only 4.35 (0.44, 45), M (SD, N); no test reported; direction is the point estimate only

outcomes.name: Number of ideas
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of all ideas a participant generated (208 ideas in total in Study 1). No test reported.

contrasts.reported: LLM-assisted human 2.71 (1.90, 45) vs Human-only 1.91 (1.40, 45), M (SD, N); no test reported; direction is the point estimate only

studies.label: Study 2 (narrow task: EdTech startup ideas, Prolific UK entrepreneurs)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Exposure to 4 education-related startup ideas drawn at random (different for each participant) from 44 ideas generated by the same fine-tuned GPT-3 model, shown as optional inspiration, versus no ideas
assignment.quote: As in Study 1, we deployed a one-way between-subjects experimental design. Participants were randomly assigned to one of two groups: use of LLM-generated ideas (n = 60) versus no use (n = 60).
assignment.prereg_locator: No preregistration mentioned; power considerations repeated from Study 1 (p. 9, Section 5.1)

arms.name: LLM-assisted human
arms.description: Saw 4 random fine-tuned-GPT-3 education startup ideas on the submission page, labelled as AI suggestions, 'Be free to ignore if not useful'

arms.name: Human-only
arms.description: Same EdTech scenario and instructions with no AI ideas

participants.exclusions: Three participants and five ideas excluded 'because of unrelatedness to the task at hand'; the paper says including them leaves breadth and depth results qualitatively unchanged. Analyzed: 59 LLM-assisted, 58 human-only. A sensitivity analysis drops manipulation-check failures (8 percent did not confirm the AI source); results said to be unchanged, no numbers printed.
participants.who: Prolific Academic United Kingdom panel members, pre-screened on approval rate and English; all self-declared current engagement in entrepreneurship or owning a business; mean age about 43; more than 90 percent born in the UK; 51 percent female.
participants.quote: Five ideas and three participants were excluded from the final analysis because of unrelatedness to the task at hand
participants.locator: p. 9, Section 5.1; p. 9, Section 5.5 ('In total, 117 participants (59 in the LLM-assisted condition and 58 in the human-only condition) generated 183 ideas.'); p. 11, Table 6

ai_tool.name_model: Same fine-tuned GPT-3 startup-idea generator as Study 1 ('Startup Ideas powered by OpenAI'); run before the public release of generative AI models
ai_tool.how_used: 44 education-related ideas selected from the model's output formed the database; each treated participant saw 4 drawn at random, as optional inspiration. No interaction with the model.

task.description: Imagine launching a startup on the use of technology in education: submit different startup ideas, each stating the need, target customer, technological solution, and expected source of revenue (Appendix B, p. 14).
task.duration: Minimum 8 minutes, instructed to spend about 10 minutes; complete participation lasted about 11 minutes (p. 9, Section 5.4)

outcomes.name: Breadth of exploration
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Number of distinct semantic categories (11 categories, one of them 'out of instruction scope') spanned by a participant's ideas. One author coded all ideas; an external researcher reviewed the ideas and the coding. No inter-rater statistic printed for Study 2. Kruskal-Wallis test; parametric test said to agree.

contrasts.reported: LLM-assisted human M = 1.39 (SD 0.70, N = 59) vs Human-only M = 1.38 (SD 0.67, N = 58); Cohen's d = 0.01; Kruskal-Wallis chi2(1) = 0.00, p = 1.00

outcomes.name: Depth of exploration
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Number of ideas divided by breadth of exploration (ideas per semantic category). Kruskal-Wallis test.

contrasts.reported: LLM-assisted human M = 1.16 (SD 0.48, N = 59) vs Human-only M = 1.11 (SD 0.35, N = 58); Cohen's d = 0.12; Kruskal-Wallis chi2(1) = 0.07, p = 0.79

outcomes.name: Average pairwise semantic similarity of ideas within condition
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Analysis 'parallel to those in Study 1' (SpaCy embeddings, pairwise cosine similarity within condition); Table 7 lists N (ideas) = 59 and 58, which matches one idea per participant, but the Study 2 text does not restate the first-idea rule. Exploratory. Sign reversed (lower similarity = more diverse).

contrasts.reported: Cosine similarity: Human-only M = 0.87 (SD = 0.04) vs LLM-assisted M = 0.87 (SD = 0.05); M difference = 0.01, 95% CI [-0.00, 0.02], p = 0.09, Cohen's d = 0.31 (permutation test, 10,000 iterations). Table 7: N (ideas) 59 and 58; permutation p = 0.09. Note: 'mean_difference_se' stands for a mean difference with a CI; no SE is printed.

diversity_detail.metric: Mean pairwise cosine similarity of sentence embeddings within condition (higher = more homogeneous)
diversity_detail.embedding_model: SpaCy sentence embeddings (model not named), as in Study 1
diversity_detail.computed_over: All pairs of ideas within a condition; 59 and 58 ideas per arm per Table 7
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Permutation test with 10,000 iterations; 95% CI and Cohen's d reported
diversity_detail.notes: Pool of LLM stimuli: M = 0.77, SD = 0.10 (p. 10), not a participant output.

outcomes.name: Average novelty (expert ratings)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two expert judges (entrepreneurship department director; management researcher) each rated all 183 ideas on seven-point scales (newness, uniqueness, unusualness). Judges discussed discrepancies before final aggregation because initial agreement on usefulness was insufficient. Descriptive and exploratory; no test reported.

contrasts.reported: LLM-assisted human 4.61 (0.87, 59) vs Human-only 4.41 (0.91, 58), M (SD, N); no test reported; direction is the point estimate only

outcomes.name: Average usefulness (expert ratings)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Feasibility and operability items; same two judges; discrepancies discussed before aggregation. No test reported.

contrasts.reported: LLM-assisted human 5.11 (1.04, 59) vs Human-only 4.60 (1.16, 58), M (SD, N); no test reported; direction is the point estimate only

outcomes.name: Average creativity (mean of expert novelty and usefulness)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Composite: mean of novelty and usefulness ratings. No test reported.

contrasts.reported: LLM-assisted human 4.86 (0.74, 59) vs Human-only 4.52 (0.88, 58), M (SD, N); no test reported; direction is the point estimate only

outcomes.name: Number of ideas
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of all ideas a participant generated (183 ideas in total in Study 2). No test reported.

contrasts.reported: LLM-assisted human 1.61 (1.02, 59) vs Human-only 1.52 (0.78, 58), M (SD, N); no test reported; direction is the point estimate only

company_involvement.description: Authors declare no competing interests (p. 13). The AI ideas come from a third-party site, 'Startup Ideas powered by OpenAI' (ideasai.net); the document does not say any company took part in the study.
company_involvement.locator: p. 13, Declaration of competing interest; p. 6, Section 4.2

data_and_code.data_url: Data will be made available on request (p. 19)

eligibility.reason: Both studies randomly assign individuals to see LLM-generated ideas (ideas_supplied) or none during an idea-generation task. People analyzed: 90 in Study 1 (93 randomized) and 117 in Study 2 (120 randomized), both above 50. Outcomes are scored on the ideas participants wrote: category counts coded by raters, embedding similarity, and expert novelty and usefulness ratings. Caveat: the AI is a pre-ChatGPT GPT-3 generator whose ideas were produced in advance; participants never interacted with it.

one_line_finding: Seeing LLM-generated startup ideas raised breadth of exploration in a broad task (Study 1: 2.32 vs 1.60 categories, d = 0.67, Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.01; Table 4, p. 9) and lowered cross-participant idea similarity (0.74 vs 0.81, p = 0.00; Table 7, p. 11), but had no effect in a narrow EdTech task (Study 2: 1.39 vs 1.38, d = 0.01, p = 1.00; Table 6, p. 11).
open_questions: Design class for Study 1: participants were master's students recruited by cold e-mail who took the study online and unsupervised, not an online panel; coded online_rct here.
Per-arm exclusions in Study 1 are implied by 46/47 randomized and 45/45 analyzed but the paper does not state them by arm.
Expert-rating outcomes (Appendix D) report only arm means, SDs and Ns, with no test; Study 2 ratings were aggregated after judges discussed discrepancies.
Study 2 similarity analysis: the text does not restate the first-idea-only rule; Table 7 Ns (59, 58 ideas) suggest it.
Similarity SDs (0.08, 0.13 etc.) are presumably over pairs of ideas; the paper does not say so.
notes: The two studies differ in task breadth, population, number of AI ideas shown (10 vs 4), and AI idea pool (453 vs 44); the paper warns against cross-study causal comparisons (p. 13, Section 7). The 'fine-tuning' is described as prompting with upvoted and downvoted ideas (Appendix A, p. 13). Manipulation check: 78 percent (Study 1) and 92 percent (Study 2) confirmed the ideas were AI-generated. No AI-versus-human outcome is coded; the paper compares human-only ideas with the pool of LLM stimuli in both studies (Study 1: M difference -0.10, 95% CI [-0.12, -0.09], d = -1.74, p. 8; Study 2: pool M = 0.77, SD = 0.10, p. 10).
